title: Disk Scheduling Algorithms
summary: Ordering the disk arm's movement to minimize seek time on rotational media — FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK — and why nearly none of it matters on an SSD.

slides.markdown:
A spinning disk has one read/write head that must physically move to a target cylinder before it can read or write — a **seek** that costs milliseconds. When many requests are queued at once, the order you service them in changes total seek distance dramatically. **Disk scheduling algorithms** decide that order.

This is a classic OS-course topic, but interviewers ask about it for a real reason: it's a concrete, numbers-driven case study in a trade-off that appears everywhere in systems — throughput vs fairness — and knowing when it stops mattering (SSDs) separates rote memorization from real understanding.

slides.sectionTitle: Why disk scheduling matters: seek time dominates HDD performance
slides.markdown:
On a spinning HDD, a **seek** — physically moving the read/write head to a different cylinder — takes roughly 4-10ms on commodity drives, plus **rotational latency** (waiting for the right sector to rotate under the head, up to one full rotation, ~4-8ms at 7200 RPM). Actually transferring data once positioned is comparatively fast. This means for workloads with many small, scattered requests, the disk spends far more time seeking than transferring — the order requests are served in can change total completion time by an order of magnitude.

With multiple pending requests queued (common under real load — many processes reading different files concurrently), the OS's disk scheduler decides which to service next, and that decision is the single biggest lever on HDD throughput under contention.

**First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)** services requests in the exact order they arrived, with zero reordering logic. It's trivially simple and perfectly fair by arrival order — no request can ever be starved by a later one jumping the queue.

The cost: with requests arriving from many unrelated processes, cylinder numbers in the queue are essentially random relative to each other, so FCFS can send the head swinging back and forth across the disk in an arbitrary, worst-case pattern — servicing cylinder 5, then 190, then 12, then 175, each swing costing a nearly full-disk seek that a smarter order could have avoided entirely.

slides.sectionTitle: Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF) — and its starvation risk
slides.markdown:
**SSTF** always services whichever pending request is physically closest to the head's current position, minimizing each individual seek. This is greedy and locally optimal — and it reliably beats FCFS on total seek distance for a fixed batch of requests.

The flaw is starvation: if requests keep arriving near the head's current position, a request sitting far away can be repeatedly skipped in favor of closer, later-arriving ones, waiting indefinitely. This is the same class of problem as [shortest-job-first process scheduling](fcfs-and-sjf) starving long jobs — greedy-by-distance (or by size) always risks starving whatever's inconveniently large or far away.

**SCAN** moves the head in one direction, servicing every pending request it passes along the way, all the way to the end of the disk, then reverses direction and does the same sweep back — exactly like a building elevator that keeps going up, serving every floor with a waiting passenger, before reversing.

This eliminates SSTF's starvation risk: every request gets serviced within at most one full sweep, since the head physically passes every cylinder each pass. It sacrifices some raw efficiency versus SSTF's greedy nearest-first choice, in exchange for a hard bound on worst-case wait time.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: SCAN sweeping like an elevator
slides.markdown:
![SCAN algorithm sweeping disk cylinders](assets/scan-sweep-cylinders.svg)

Notice the head travels all the way to cylinder 199 even if the last actual request was at 175 — pure SCAN commits to reaching the disk's physical end before reversing, which is the specific inefficiency C-SCAN and LOOK (next slides) each fix differently.

Every request gets a checkmark within one full sweep in each direction — the structural guarantee against starvation that FCFS and SSTF don't provide.

slides.sectionTitle: C-SCAN — uniform wait time via one-direction scanning
slides.markdown:
**C-SCAN (Circular SCAN)** sweeps in only one direction — say, always low-to-high — servicing requests along the way; upon reaching the end, it jumps immediately back to the start (without servicing anything on that return jump) and begins the same one-direction sweep again. Treating the disk as circular this way gives every cylinder a much more **uniform** wait time than plain SCAN, where cylinders near the reversal point get serviced twice in quick succession (once on each pass) while cylinders in the middle wait almost a full cycle.

The cost is the "wasted" return jump — physically repositioning the head across the whole disk without doing any useful work during that traversal.

slides.sectionTitle: LOOK and C-LOOK — not going all the way to the end
slides.markdown:
Plain SCAN and C-SCAN both commit to physically reaching the disk's outer edge (cylinder 0 or the max cylinder) even if no pending request lies anywhere near there. **LOOK** fixes this for SCAN: it reverses direction as soon as there are no more requests ahead of it in the current direction, rather than continuing to the physical end. **C-LOOK** applies the same fix to C-SCAN — jump back to the lowest pending request, not all the way to cylinder 0.

This is a small change with a real payoff: in a workload where requests cluster in a narrower band of cylinders (common — a single application's data often isn't spread across the entire disk), LOOK/C-LOOK avoid the wasted travel to and from the true physical extremes, which is why they're what real disk schedulers actually implement rather than pure SCAN/C-SCAN.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: total head movement compared across algorithms
slides.markdown:
For a request queue of cylinders `[98, 183, 41, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67]` with the head starting at cylinder **53**, on a 0-199 disk:

```text
FCFS:  53->98->183->41->122->14->124->65->67
       total movement = 45+85+142+81+108+110+59+2 = 632

SSTF:  53->65->67->41->14->98->122->124->183
       total movement = 12+2+26+27+84+24+2+59 = 236

SCAN (moving toward 199 first):
       53->65->67->98->122->124->183->199->41->14
       total movement = (199-53) + (199-14) = 146+185 = 331

C-LOOK (moving toward 199 first, wraps to lowest pending):
       53->65->67->98->122->124->183 -> [jump] -> 14->41
       total movement = (183-53) + (183-14) + (41-14) = 130+169+27 = 326
```

SSTF wins this specific batch on raw total movement — but recall its starvation risk under continuous arrivals, which this static, one-shot comparison can't show.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: SSTF vs SCAN vs C-SCAN
slides.markdown:
| | SSTF | SCAN | C-SCAN |
|---|---|---|---|
| Optimizes for | Minimum seek per step (greedy) | Bounded worst-case wait (one sweep) | Uniform wait time across all cylinders |
| Starvation risk | Yes — far requests can be perpetually skipped | No | No |
| Wait time variance | High — depends entirely on request arrival pattern | Moderate — cylinders near reversal points wait less | Low — every cylinder waits roughly one full circular pass |
| Wasted travel | None inherent | To the physical disk end even with no nearby requests | To the physical disk end, plus the return jump |

**How to decide:** SSTF wins raw throughput for a batch workload without starvation risk (e.g., a one-time defrag pass); SCAN/LOOK variants are the right default for a live, continuously-arriving request stream where fairness matters — which is why production disk schedulers use LOOK-family algorithms, not pure SSTF.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: applying HDD scheduling logic to SSDs
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Disk scheduling algorithms like SCAN and C-LOOK are universally important for storage performance."

**Why it's wrong:** every algorithm on this page exists to minimize **seek distance** — a cost that only exists because an HDD has a physical arm that must move. An SSD has no moving parts and no meaningfully different cost for accessing cylinder 5 versus cylinder 50,000; any flash page is electrically addressable in roughly constant time. Reordering requests by physical proximity optimizes for a cost that simply doesn't exist on this hardware.

**Correct model:** for SSDs, Linux's default I/O scheduler (`none`/`noop`, or `mq-deadline` for basic fairness) deliberately does far less reordering than the HDD-era `CFQ`/`deadline` schedulers, because seek-minimizing logic is pure overhead with zero benefit on flash — a genuinely different scheduling problem (wear leveling, parallelism across flash channels, covered in [SSDs & Modern Storage I/O](ssd-and-modern-storage-io)) replaces it.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: I/O scheduling still matters on SSDs, just for different reasons
slides.markdown:
Dropping seek-minimization doesn't mean SSDs need zero scheduling — it means the goals shift entirely. Modern NVMe SSDs support many parallel command queues (thousands of outstanding requests across multiple hardware queues), so the scheduling question becomes **how much reordering/merging is worth the CPU cost of doing it**, not **which cylinder is closest**. Linux's `mq-deadline` still enforces basic per-request latency bounds (preventing any single request from waiting arbitrarily long) without HDD-era seek logic; `none` skips scheduling almost entirely, betting that the SSD's own internal parallelism handles ordering better than software guessing would.

A staff-level answer distinguishes these: "scheduling doesn't matter for SSDs" is an oversimplification of "seek-distance-based scheduling doesn't matter for SSDs" — the underlying problem (deciding request order and priority under queueing) persists, just with a completely different cost model to optimize against.
